payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage

Fluency, Experience, and the Creek Trail
Ines Varlow, opinion column in the Halvering Courier-Ledger (fictional)

When the Pell Hollow school district announced that eighth graders would spend the spring restoring a neglected creek trail instead of completing nightly worksheets, the complaints arrived before the shovels did. Parents asked how anyone would know whether their children could still factor a polynomial. The superintendent answered that a child who has spent forty hours persuading a town council to fund a footbridge has learned something no worksheet measures. Both sides, I think, are half right. Homework, at its best, is practice: the small, repetitive, private labor by which a skill becomes reliable. A community project is something else: public, slow, dependent on other people, and often a mess. The question is not which one is nobler. It is whether a school owes its students fluency, or experience, or some ratio of the two that nobody has yet agreed on, and whether that ratio should be set by the people who grade the work or by the people who live with the results.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt:
In a column for a regional newspaper, education commentator Ines Varlow responded to a school district's decision to let a long-term community project take the place of part of students' nightly homework. Her column is reproduced below as Source A.

After reading the passage, write an essay that argues your position on the extent to which schools should replace some traditional homework with long-term community projects.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible position.
- Provide evidence to support your line of reasoning; evidence may come from your reading, your experience, or your observation.
- Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning, and use appropriate grammar and punctuation in communicating your argument.
parts.model_answer:
When Pell Hollow traded worksheets for a creek trail, the parents who worried about polynomials were asking the right question about the wrong subject. Ines Varlow is right that homework is "practice" and a community project is "experience," but she writes as if the two are competing for the same hour of a student's night. They aren't, at least not always. Schools should replace traditional homework with long-term projects only where the homework was never building fluency in the first place, and they should keep the nightly practice that skills like algebra or a foreign language actually need. Even then, the replacement only works if the project is designed for the students who have the least free time, not the most.

Some homework really is the "small, repetitive, private labor" Varlow describes. Last fall in Algebra II I spent most of a week doing thirty logarithm problems a night, and I hated it. But by the Thursday quiz I could rewrite log base 2 of 32 without thinking, and that only happened because I had gotten the same kind of problem wrong maybe fifteen times, alone at my kitchen table. No footbridge campaign would have given me that. A project might use math, like measuring a trail's slope or budgeting lumber, but it uses math a student already has. It doesn't drill it. If a district cut this kind of homework for a project, it would be giving up the one thing the project itself depends on.

A lot of homework, though, isn't practice at all. In my U.S. History class we answered ten comprehension questions for every textbook section, and most people copied the answers from the bold words in the chapter. The assignment measured completion, not thinking. Compare that to what my cousin did at her school in Marlow County. Her class spent a semester recording interviews with people who worked at the old shoe factory before it closed, and then they built a display for the public library. She had to figure out which questions got a nervous seventy-year-old man to open up, check his dates against newspaper archives, and decide what to cut. That is the skill history homework says it teaches, evaluating sources and building an argument from them, except she actually did it. Here the project doesn't replace practice; it replaces a fake version of practice with the real thing. So the line for replacement isn't between subjects like "math" and "history." It's between assignments that build a skill and assignments that only prove time was spent.

The strongest objection to projects is not that they are messy, which Varlow already admits, but that they are unequal. Freshman year our biology class did a water-testing project at Grant Pond that was supposed to replace a month of lab worksheets. Within two weeks it was obvious which groups had a parent who could drive them to the pond on Saturdays and which had members working shifts at the grocery store. The kids with jobs ended up making the poster while everyone else did the science, and the grades showed it. A worksheet, for all its boredom, can be done at 11 p.m. after a shift. If schools replace homework with projects, they have to put the project hours inside the school day or provide rides, or else "experience" turns into something only students with free afternoons can afford.

That is also my answer to Varlow's last question about who sets the ratio. The people who grade the work know which assignments are busywork, but the people who "live with the results" include students whose evenings are already full. A school should decide subject by subject, and really assignment by assignment, with both groups in the room. The creek trail may be worth forty hours. Just not the forty hours a kid needed to learn to factor a polynomial, and not forty hours that only part of the class could show up for.

rubric_rows.criterion: The thesis must take a position on extent, not just on whether community projects are good or whether homework is bad. 'Community projects teach valuable skills' is not yet a thesis; 'Community projects should replace homework only in subjects where the skill being practiced is the same skill the project demands' is. A thesis that argues the ratio should be decided locally by families and teachers rather than fixed by policy is also defensible, since the column explicitly raises the question of who decides.

Evidence may be personal (a service project that worked or collapsed, a homework routine that built or failed to build a skill), observed (a sibling's school, a local program), or drawn from reading. Evidence counts as specific when a grader can picture it: a named kind of task, a concrete outcome, a particular difficulty. Using the column as evidence is acceptable but not required; an essay that only paraphrases Varlow's creek trail example without adding anything earns at most a 2 on this row. Commentary must explain the link to extent, for instance why a given example shows that projects can replace practice in one domain but not another.

A qualified thesis alone does not earn this point; the qualification must be developed. An essay that notices the column's final question about who sets the ratio, and builds an argument around it, is a strong candidate. So is an essay that argues the counterintuitive case (for example, that long projects should replace homework more in mathematics than in social studies, with reasons) and sustains it.

   - 4: Provides specific, well-chosen evidence and consistently explains how it supports the claim; the line of reasoning is clear and each paragraph advances it rather than repeating it.    - 3: Provides specific evidence for the position and explains how most of it supports the line of reasoning.    - 2: Provides some specific evidence (a remembered assignment, a described project, a book or news story, an observed classroom) but the commentary is thin or repetitive, often just asserting that the example 'shows' the point.    - 1: Offers evidence that is mostly general or unrelated to the position (for example, a vague claim that 'students learn more by doing' with no specific example), and the commentary, if any, does not explain how the evidence supports the claim. Often reads as a list of opinions.
   - 0: Restates the thesis or the column, or offers only general statements with no evidence at all.
Sophistication (0-1): A qualified thesis alone does not earn this point; the qualification must be developed. An essay that notices the column's final question about who sets the ratio, and builds an argument around it, is a strong candidate. So is an essay that argues the counterintuitive case (for example, that long projects should replace homework more in mathematics than in social studies, with reasons) and sustains it.
   - 1: The essay does at least one of the following in a sustained way, not as a single sentence: it complicates the question by distinguishing kinds of homework, kinds of projects, or kinds of students for whom the trade-off differs; it examines the hidden assumptions in the debate (for example, that fluency and experience are measurable on the same scale, or that 'the community' benefits equally from student labor); it considers the costs of its own position honestly (such as the inequity when projects depend on transportation or free afternoons); or it situates the question in a broader context about what schools are for. The prose is controlled and the voice is consistent.
   - 0: The argument is sound but flat: it does not complicate its own position, treats homework or projects as uniformly good or bad, uses the counterargument only as a token to dismiss, or relies on sweeping generalizations and ornamental language that does not advance thought.
Note: Score the essay as a whole for row B; do not add points per paragraph.
Note: An essay that argues against any replacement at all is fully defensible and should be scored on its evidence and reasoning, not on agreement with the column.
Note: Essays that drift into arguing homework should be abolished entirely can still earn thesis credit if they explicitly connect that claim to community projects as the replacement; otherwise treat the thesis as off-task.
Note: Length is not a criterion. A short essay with precise evidence and clear commentary can earn a 4 on row B.

Schools should replace some homework with long-term community projects, but only in subjects like science and social studies where the project actually uses what students are learning. In math and writing, where skills depend on repeated practice, projects should not take over the nightly work.

When I was in Algebra I, I did not really understand factoring until I did about twenty problems in a row one night and finally saw the pattern. If the Pell Hollow students spend the whole spring on the creek trail, some of them might forget how to factor a polynomial, which is what the parents were worried about. So in math I think homework has to stay, because the fluency comes from the repetition.

On the other hand, there are subjects where a project teaches more than a worksheet. My cousin's school in another town had an environmental science class that tested the water in a local pond every month for a year. They had to collect samples, record numbers, and write a report for the town. He learned how to use a graph because he needed one, and he remembered the data much better than he remembered any worksheet. It is whether a school owes its students fluency, or experience, or some ratio of the two that nobody has yet agreed on, and whether that ratio should be set by the people who grade the work or by the people who live with the results.

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No thesis, or a thesis that merely restates the prompt (for example, 'Schools should think carefully about whether to replace homework with community projects'), or a statement that only summarizes Varlow's column, or a thesis that answers a different question (such as whether homework should exist at all) without connecting it to the replacement question.
descriptors.1: A defensible, specific claim about how far schools should go in substituting long-term community projects for traditional homework. The claim may be a full endorsement, a full rejection, or a qualified position (for instance, replacement is appropriate only in certain subjects, grade levels, or proportions, or only when particular conditions are met). The thesis may appear anywhere in the essay and may be more than one sentence.

rows.task_specific: The thesis must take a position on extent, not just on whether community projects are good or whether homework is bad. 'Community projects teach valuable skills' is not yet a thesis; 'Community projects should replace homework only in subjects where the skill being practiced is the same skill the project demands' is. A thesis that argues the ratio should be decided locally by families and teachers rather than fixed by policy is also defensible, since the column explicitly raises the question of who decides.

rows.name: Evidence and Commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis or the column, or offers only general statements with no evidence at all.
descriptors.1: Offers evidence that is mostly general or unrelated to the position (for example, a vague claim that 'students learn more by doing' with no specific example), and the commentary, if any, does not explain how the evidence supports the claim. Often reads as a list of opinions.
descriptors.2: Provides some specific evidence (a remembered assignment, a described project, a book or news story, an observed classroom) but the commentary is thin or repetitive, often just asserting that the example 'shows' the point. The line of reasoning may be present but is not consistently developed; paragraphs may feel interchangeable.
descriptors.3: Provides specific evidence for the position and explains how most of it supports the line of reasoning. The essay moves in a recognizable order (for example, establishing what homework is for, then what projects do, then where the two overlap or conflict). Some commentary may be uneven, or one piece of evidence may be left to speak for itself.
descriptors.4: Provides specific, well-chosen evidence and consistently explains how it supports the claim; the line of reasoning is clear and each paragraph advances it rather than repeating it. The essay treats the question of extent directly, showing where the proposed replacement should stop and why, and it engages with at least one plausible objection or complication rather than ignoring it.

rows.task_specific: Evidence may be personal (a service project that worked or collapsed, a homework routine that built or failed to build a skill), observed (a sibling's school, a local program), or drawn from reading. Evidence counts as specific when a grader can picture it: a named kind of task, a concrete outcome, a particular difficulty. Using the column as evidence is acceptable but not required; an essay that only paraphrases Varlow's creek trail example without adding anything earns at most a 2 on this row. Commentary must explain the link to extent, for instance why a given example shows that projects can replace practice in one domain but not another.

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: The argument is sound but flat: it does not complicate its own position, treats homework or projects as uniformly good or bad, uses the counterargument only as a token to dismiss, or relies on sweeping generalizations and ornamental language that does not advance thought.
descriptors.1: The essay does at least one of the following in a sustained way, not as a single sentence: it complicates the question by distinguishing kinds of homework, kinds of projects, or kinds of students for whom the trade-off differs; it examines the hidden assumptions in the debate (for example, that fluency and experience are measurable on the same scale, or that 'the community' benefits equally from student labor); it considers the costs of its own position honestly (such as the inequity when projects depend on transportation or free afternoons); or it situates the question in a broader context about what schools are for. The prose is controlled and the voice is consistent.

rows.task_specific: A qualified thesis alone does not earn this point; the qualification must be developed. An essay that notices the column's final question about who sets the ratio, and builds an argument around it, is a strong candidate. So is an essay that argues the counterintuitive case (for example, that long projects should replace homework more in mathematics than in social studies, with reasons) and sustains it.

scoring_notes: Score the essay as a whole for row B; do not add points per paragraph.
An essay that argues against any replacement at all is fully defensible and should be scored on its evidence and reasoning, not on agreement with the column.

Essays that drift into arguing homework should be abolished entirely can still earn thesis credit if they explicitly connect that claim to community projects as the replacement; otherwise treat the thesis as off-task.
Length is not a criterion. A short essay with precise evidence and clear commentary can earn a 4 on row B.
Do not award the sophistication point for vocabulary or for a dramatic opening; award it only for complexity of thought that runs through the argument.

defensible_positions: Schools should replace a substantial share of homework with long-term community projects because sustained public work teaches persistence, communication, and civic judgment that private practice cannot.
Schools should keep most homework as it is, because repetitive practice is the only reliable way to build fluency, and projects should be added, not substituted.
Replacement is appropriate only where the skill the project demands is the same skill the homework was meant to practice (writing, measurement, research), and not where it is not.
The ratio should be decided locally by teachers, families, and students rather than fixed by district policy, because the costs of projects fall unevenly.
Projects should replace homework mainly in older grades, after fluency has been established, and sparingly in younger grades.
Long projects should replace homework more aggressively than most people assume, because much nightly homework is not practice at all but busywork, and the real loss is small.
lines_of_reasoning: Define what homework actually accomplishes when it works (fluency through repetition), then show which subjects depend on that and which do not; conclude that replacement should track that distinction.

Argue from the nature of long-term work: deadlines months away, dependence on other people, visible public results; show that these features build capacities schools claim to value but rarely assess, and therefore justify replacing a meaningful fraction of homework.
Argue from equity: projects require time, transport, and adult support that are unequally distributed, so replacement should be limited or paired with in-school time.

Argue from the question of who decides, following the column's closing line: since the people who grade the work and the people who live with it want different things, the ratio should be negotiated rather than imposed.

Argue the counterintuitive case that the subject most people would protect, mathematics, is actually where a long project (budgeting a footbridge, measuring a trail) can replace worksheets most fully, while subjects like literature depend on private, repeated reading that a project cannot substitute.

Argue from the risk of mess: the column admits projects are 'often a mess,' and a mess can be formative or merely wasteful depending on whether a teacher has time to turn it into learning; so replacement should be scaled to staffing, not to ideals.

rhetorical_choices.effect: Opens with a concrete local dispute so the abstract question has faces and stakes; students may use or extend this example.
Signals that the column will not pick a side, which models the qualified positions students are invited to take.
Defines homework as practice and projects as public, slow, dependent work, giving students two categories to accept, refine, or challenge.
Reframes the debate from nobility to proportion and authority, opening the question of who should set the ratio.

source_uses.usable_for: The creek trail and footbridge example as a concrete case; the definitions of homework as practice and projects as public and slow; the closing question about fluency versus experience and about who decides the ratio. Students may adopt, qualify, or reject Varlow's framing, but must add evidence of their own.

common_pitfalls: Arguing about whether homework is good or bad in general instead of about the extent to which projects should replace it.
Treating 'community projects' as automatically virtuous and offering no account of what students would stop practicing.
Relying entirely on Varlow's creek trail example instead of supplying evidence of one's own.
Writing a thesis that says 'there should be a balance' without saying where the balance lies or how it would be decided.
Presenting a counterargument in one sentence and dismissing it in the next without engaging it.
Using hypothetical students ('imagine a student who...') as the only evidence, with no grounding in reading, experience, or observation.
Ignoring practical complications (who supervises, who provides transport, how the work is assessed) that a thoughtful position would need to address.
Confusing a community project with ordinary group work or a single afternoon of volunteering, which misreads the long-term aspect of the prompt.

samples.essay:
When Pell Hollow traded worksheets for a creek trail, the parents who worried about polynomials were asking the right question about the wrong subject. Ines Varlow is right that homework is "practice" and a community project is "experience," but she writes as if the two are competing for the same hour of a student's night. They aren't, at least not always. Schools should replace traditional homework with long-term projects only where the homework was never building fluency in the first place, and they should keep the nightly practice that skills like algebra or a foreign language actually need. Even then, the replacement only works if the project is designed for the students who have the least free time, not the most.

Some homework really is the "small, repetitive, private labor" Varlow describes. Last fall in Algebra II I spent most of a week doing thirty logarithm problems a night, and I hated it. But by the Thursday quiz I could rewrite log base 2 of 32 without thinking, and that only happened because I had gotten the same kind of problem wrong maybe fifteen times, alone at my kitchen table. No footbridge campaign would have given me that. A project might use math, like measuring a trail's slope or budgeting lumber, but it uses math a student already has. It doesn't drill it. If a district cut this kind of homework for a project, it would be giving up the one thing the project itself depends on.

A lot of homework, though, isn't practice at all. In my U.S. History class we answered ten comprehension questions for every textbook section, and most people copied the answers from the bold words in the chapter. The assignment measured completion, not thinking. Compare that to what my cousin did at her school in Marlow County. Her class spent a semester recording interviews with people who worked at the old shoe factory before it closed, and then they built a display for the public library. She had to figure out which questions got a nervous seventy-year-old man to open up, check his dates against newspaper archives, and decide what to cut. That is the skill history homework says it teaches, evaluating sources and building an argument from them, except she actually did it. Here the project doesn't replace practice; it replaces a fake version of practice with the real thing. So the line for replacement isn't between subjects like "math" and "history." It's between assignments that build a skill and assignments that only prove time was spent.

The strongest objection to projects is not that they are messy, which Varlow already admits, but that they are unequal. Freshman year our biology class did a water-testing project at Grant Pond that was supposed to replace a month of lab worksheets. Within two weeks it was obvious which groups had a parent who could drive them to the pond on Saturdays and which had members working shifts at the grocery store. The kids with jobs ended up making the poster while everyone else did the science, and the grades showed it. A worksheet, for all its boredom, can be done at 11 p.m. after a shift. If schools replace homework with projects, they have to put the project hours inside the school day or provide rides, or else "experience" turns into something only students with free afternoons can afford.

That is also my answer to Varlow's last question about who sets the ratio. The people who grade the work know which assignments are busywork, but the people who "live with the results" include students whose evenings are already full. A school should decide subject by subject, and really assignment by assignment, with both groups in the room. The creek trail may be worth forty hours. Just not the forty hours a kid needed to learn to factor a polynomial, and not forty hours that only part of the class could show up for.

Schools should replace some homework with long-term community projects, but only in subjects like science and social studies where the project actually uses what students are learning. In math and writing, where skills depend on repeated practice, projects should not take over the nightly work.

Ines Varlow says homework is "practice" and a community project is "something else," and I think that is true. Practice is what makes a skill reliable. When I was in Algebra I, I did not really understand factoring until I did about twenty problems in a row one night and finally saw the pattern. A community project could not have given me that, because a project does not repeat the same step enough times. If the Pell Hollow students spend the whole spring on the creek trail, some of them might forget how to factor a polynomial, which is what the parents were worried about. So in math I think homework has to stay, because the fluency comes from the repetition.

On the other hand, there are subjects where a project teaches more than a worksheet. My cousin's school in another town had an environmental science class that tested the water in a local pond every month for a year. They had to collect samples, record numbers, and write a report for the town. He learned how to use a graph because he needed one, and he remembered the data much better than he remembered any worksheet. This shows that when the project requires the same skill the class is teaching, it can replace the homework, since the students are practicing anyway but with a real purpose. The superintendent in the column is right that persuading a town council teaches something a worksheet does not, but that is mostly a speaking and civics skill, so it fits best in a social studies class.

Some people would say projects are unfair because not every student has a ride or free afternoons. That is a real problem. A student who works after school or lives far from the site cannot put in forty hours the way another student can. For this reason schools should give class time for the project and not make it all extra work at home. If they cannot do that, then the project should be a smaller part of the grade.

In the end, the extent of replacement should depend on the subject and not be one rule for the whole district. Varlow asks who should set the ratio, and I think teachers should, since they know whether the project and the skill match. Projects can replace part of homework, but not all of it, and not in every class.

prompt.scenario: Across many towns and cities, parks departments are being asked to replace or supplement ordinary shade trees with fruit and nut trees on public land such as parks, school grounds, medians and sidewalk planting strips, and to invite residents to pick what grows. sources.title: Five Seasons In, Marlow Bend Weighs the Harvest on Orchard Boulevard
sources.attribution: Teodora Vask, staff reporter, The Pell River Ledger, 2024
sources.body:
When Marlow Bend replaced 340 dying ash trees along Orchard Boulevard with plums, pawpaws, hazelnuts and serviceberries in 2019, the city council called it the first edible street in the region. Five seasons later the branches are bearing, and so are the complaints.

The parks department logged 212 service requests related to the trees last year, most of them about fallen plums staining sidewalks and drawing wasps in late August. Yet the same department counted eleven neighborhood harvest days, organized by a volunteer group that calls itself the Boulevard Gleaners, which carried roughly 2,300 pounds of fruit to two church pantries before it could rot on the pavement.

"The trees that have a block captain look great," said parks superintendent Imani Threlkeld. "The ones that don't look like nobody loves them, because nobody does." Her department's figures show that a fruit tree on a block with a volunteer steward costs the city about 71 dollars a year to maintain, compared with 48 dollars for an ordinary shade tree and 112 dollars for a fruit tree on a block with no steward at all.

Council member Rufus Adebanjo-Lind, who voted for the program, now wants new plantings limited to parks and school grounds rather than sidewalks. "A plum tree over a bus stop was a mistake," he said. "A plum tree beside a playground is a gift." The council takes up his proposal next month, and both the Gleaners and a group of Orchard Boulevard shop owners have asked to speak.

sources.title: A Sidewalk Plum Is Not a Food Policy
sources.attribution: Corwin Ashby-Feld, opinion column, The Hollowmere Review, 2023
sources.body:
Every spring some council somewhere discovers the public orchard, and every spring I am asked to be charmed. I decline. The picture is lovely: a child on tiptoe, a grandmother with an apron full of pears, a street that feeds its own. The arithmetic is not.

A plum tree fruits for about three weeks. Hunger lasts fifty-two. A family that cannot afford groceries in February is not helped by a windfall in August that it has no way to can, freeze or store. What that family needs is money, refrigeration and a pantry that is open on Tuesdays, none of which grows on a branch.

Consider also who gets the fruit. Not the man in the wheelchair, who cannot reach it. Not the night-shift nurse, who sleeps through the two good picking days. The harvest goes to whoever has a ladder, a free Saturday and the nerve to strip a tree before the neighbors notice. We call that sharing. It looks more like a race.

Then comes the cleanup. Rotting fruit on a sidewalk is a slip hazard, a wasp buffet and, eventually, a claim against the city. A hazelnut dropped from twenty feet onto a parked windshield is a small event that produces a large letter. A city that cannot keep its ordinary maples pruned should not be volunteering to run an orchard.

Plant shade. Shade is free every year, falls on everyone equally and never needs a block captain. Then take the money you would have spent chasing plums down the gutter and give it to the food bank, which already knows what to do with it.

sources.title: Who Picks the Pears: A Conversation with Verrin Heights Parks Director Osric Palumbo
sources.attribution: Interview conducted by Nadira Quell for the Ostrander Institute for Urban Land oral history series, 2025
sources.body:
Quell: Your department has planted edible trees twice, with very different results. What happened?

Palumbo: In 2017 we put twelve pear trees in sidewalk cutouts downtown because a grant paid for them. Nobody on that street asked for them. They are the ugliest trees we own. Pears drop on the sidewalk, the merchants call us, and we send a crew with a hose. In 2021 a seniors' club at Thistle Park asked for a grove. We planted forty trees there, mostly persimmons, hazelnuts and serviceberries, and the club signed an agreement to water, pick and sweep. Those are the best trees we own.

Quell: So the difference is the people, not the trees?

Palumbo: Both. Species matters. A persimmon holds its fruit until someone takes it; a plum lets go the moment it ripens and finds the nearest shoe. We now plant only what I call polite fruit. But the agreement matters more. My rule is simple: no steward, no tree. If a group will not put its name on a two-page paper before the hole is dug, the hole does not get dug.

Quell: Critics say the harvest goes to whoever gets there first.

Palumbo: That is exactly what happens when nobody organizes it. At Thistle Park there is a chalkboard with picking dates, a shelf of loaner poles for people who cannot climb, and a standing rule that the first basket of the day goes to the pantry on Ferrow Street. None of that is complicated. All of it has to be decided before the first blossom, not after the first complaint.

Quell: Would you plant fruit trees along streets again?

Palumbo: Not in a tree pit, no. In a park, a schoolyard, a library lawn, yes, gladly, if someone has asked for it.

Palumbo: In 2017 we put twelve pear trees in sidewalk cutouts downtown because a grant paid for them.
Nobody on that street asked for them.
They are the ugliest trees we own.
Pears drop on the sidewalk, the merchants call us, and we send a crew with a hose.
In 2021 a seniors' club at Thistle Park asked for a grove.
We planted forty trees there, mostly persimmons, hazelnuts and serviceberries, and the club signed an agreement to water, pick and sweep.
Those are the best trees we own.
Quell: So the difference is the people, not the trees?
Palumbo: Both.
Species matters.
A persimmon holds its fruit until someone takes it; a plum lets go the moment it ripens and finds the nearest shoe.
We now plant only what I call polite fruit.
But the agreement matters more.
My rule is simple: no steward, no tree.
If a group will not put its name on a two-page paper before the hole is dug, the hole does not get dug.
Quell: Critics say the harvest goes to whoever gets there first.
Palumbo: That is exactly what happens when nobody organizes it.

At Thistle Park there is a chalkboard with picking dates, a shelf of loaner poles for people who cannot climb, and a standing rule that the first basket of the day goes to the pantry on Ferrow Street.
None of that is complicated.
All of it has to be decided before the first blossom, not after the first complaint.
Quell: Would you plant fruit trees along streets again?
Palumbo: Not in a tree pit, no.
In a park, a schoolyard, a library lawn, yes, gladly, if someone has asked for it.

sources.title: June, With Purple Fingers
sources.attribution: Lissette Marrow, personal essay, The Caddis Falls Almanac, 2024
sources.body:
The serviceberry outside the Caddis Falls branch library is not a remarkable tree. It is maybe fifteen feet tall, leans a little toward the bike rack, and for eleven months of the year nobody looks at it. Then June comes and it is the most important tree in the neighborhood.

My daughter was six the first time we picked. She did not believe me that the berries were food. Food, in her experience, arrived in a plastic clamshell with a sticker. I ate one in front of her. She watched me for a full minute to see if I would die, then ate four, then thirty.

That is where I met Mr. Haldane, who lives in the brick building and who had been picking that tree alone for nine years. He showed us how to bend a branch down without snapping it. He told us the berries were better with lemon. He had never spoken to me before and has not stopped since. I now know his knee is bad and his sister is in Ferndale and he does not care for the new bus route.

I will not pretend the tree is tidy. The berries stain the sidewalk, and for two weeks the birds hold a loud and messy festival in its branches. So does everything worth doing. My kitchen is a disaster after we bake. The library steps are a disaster after story hour.

What the tree gives is not really the fruit, though the fruit is good. It is the excuse. It gives a shy child and an old man a reason to stand on the same sidewalk and reach for the same branch. You cannot buy that in a clamshell. A city that plants it is planting something it will not be able to measure, which is not the same as saying it is not worth planting.

rows.name: Thesis

descriptors.0: No thesis, or a thesis that only restates the prompt ("Cities planting fruit trees has pros and cons"), only summarizes what the sources say, or takes no position the reader could disagree with. A thesis that merely announces the topic ("This essay will discuss public orchards") also earns 0.
descriptors.1: States a defensible, arguable position on whether cities should plant fruit and nut trees on public land for residents to harvest. The position may be in favor, opposed, or conditional, but a conditional thesis must name the condition (for example, "only in parks and schoolyards with a signed steward group") rather than saying "it depends." The thesis may appear anywhere in the essay and may be more than one sentence.

rows.task_specific: Defensible positions include: full support; opposition in favor of shade trees and direct food funding; support limited to parks, schoolyards and library lawns rather than sidewalks; support only where a volunteer steward group commits before planting; support for low-mess species only. A thesis that says the question "is complicated" without committing earns 0.

rows.name: Evidence and Commentary

descriptors.0: Restates the thesis, offers only personal opinion with no reference to the sources, or uses material unrelated to the prompt.
descriptors.1: Mentions or quotes material from fewer than three sources, or from three sources in a way that is mostly summary with little or no explanation of how it supports a position. Commentary, where present, repeats the source's point in different words.
descriptors.2: Uses at least three sources, but the evidence is handled unevenly: some sources are explained in relation to the thesis while others are dropped in as quotations or listed one after another ("Source A says... Source B says..."). The line of reasoning is loose; paragraphs may be organized by source rather than by the writer's own claims. Numbers from Source E or F may be cited without saying what they show.
descriptors.3: Uses at least three sources as support for a clear line of reasoning organized around the writer's own claims. Commentary consistently explains how each piece of evidence advances the position, for example by connecting the stewardship cost gap in Source F to the low volunteer willingness in Source E. Some commentary may be thin or may not fully address evidence that cuts against the thesis.
descriptors.4: Uses at least three sources with specific, well-chosen evidence that is woven into a sustained line of reasoning. Commentary consistently and explicitly explains the significance of each piece of evidence to the thesis and shows how the sources relate to one another (agreement, tension, qualification). The writer puts sources in conversation, for example using Source C's "no steward, no tree" rule to answer Source B's fairness objection, or using Source E's gap between approval (68 percent for parks) and participation (23 percent harvested) to test Source D's claims. Counterevidence is acknowledged and handled rather than ignored.

rows.task_specific: Count a source as 'used' only if the essay draws specific content from it (a claim, quotation, figure or example), not merely its letter. Sources E and F count as used when the writer cites a specific number and interprets it. Uniting evidence across text and data sources (e.g. Source A's 71/48/112 figures match Source F) is a mark of the 3-4 range. A response that reaches 4 need not use all six sources; three well-integrated sources can earn 4.

rows.name: Sophistication

descriptors.0: Prose is adequate but the argument stays at the level of pro versus con, treats every source as equally reliable, or uses sweeping generalities and ornamental language without adding to the argument. Simply including a counterargument paragraph does not by itself earn the point.
descriptors.1: Demonstrates sophistication of thought in at least one sustained way: situating the argument in a broader context (what public land is for, who public goods actually reach); explaining the limits or implications of the position (for example, that a steward requirement may concentrate orchards in neighborhoods with organized residents); weighing the differing purposes and reliability of the sources (a personal essay versus a department cost report versus an op-ed with a clear agenda); or writing in a consistently vivid, precise and persuasive style that serves the argument.

rows.task_specific: Credit, for example, an essay that notices Source B's fairness objection and Source C's loaner poles address the same problem from opposite conclusions, or that observes Source E's 32 percent unsure about safety suggests education rather than planting is the limiting factor. Do not credit a mere list of 'both sides.'

scoring_notes: Score holistically within each row; a response need not do everything listed to earn a level, but must meet the core expectation of that level.
A conditional thesis that names its condition is fully defensible and should not be scored lower than a flat yes or no.

Misreading a number (for example, saying 68 percent of residents harvested when Source E says 23 percent) does not automatically lower the score, but commentary built on a misreading cannot count as effective evidence.
Organizing paragraphs by source rather than by claim is the most common marker of a 2 in Row B.
Row C is awarded for what the essay does throughout or at a key moment, not for a single sentence of hedging in the conclusion.

defensible_positions: Cities should plant fruit and nut trees on public land and invite harvesting because the social and food benefits outweigh manageable mess and cost.
Cities should not plant edible trees on public land; they should plant shade trees and direct the savings to food banks and pantries that address hunger year-round.
Cities should plant edible trees only in parks, schoolyards and library lawns, not in sidewalk tree pits or over bus stops, where fallen fruit causes most complaints.
Cities should plant edible trees only where a resident group has formally committed to watering, picking and cleanup before the trees go in, since stewardship explains the cost gap.
Cities should proceed, but pair plantings with organized harvest systems (posted picking dates, loaner poles, pantry-first rules) so the fruit reaches people who cannot race for it.
lines_of_reasoning: Stewardship, not fruit itself, drives cost: Source F shows a stewarded fruit tree costs 71 dollars versus 112 unstewarded, so the policy question is really about organizing volunteers, which Source E suggests only 29 percent are willing to do.
Location determines outcome: Source A's council member, Source C's director and Source E's split (68 percent for parks, 41 percent for streets) converge on parks rather than sidewalks.

Equity cuts both ways: Source B argues the harvest goes to those with ladders and free Saturdays, while Source C shows that rule-setting (loaner poles, pantry-first baskets) can answer that objection.

Unmeasurable benefits still count: Source D's account of neighbors meeting over a tree, read against Source E's gap between approval and participation, raises the question of whether the benefit is food or community.

rhetorical_choices.effect: Source B's 'A plum tree fruits for about three weeks. Hunger lasts fifty-two.' compresses the op-ed's central claim that seasonal fruit cannot address year-round need.
Source A's council member contrasts the plum tree over a bus stop with the one beside a playground, giving writers a ready-made frame for a location-based position.
Source D's Mr. Haldane story makes the social benefit concrete, inviting writers to weigh narrative evidence against statistical evidence.
Source D admits the mess and answers it with 'So does everything worth doing,' modeling how a writer can concede a cost without abandoning a position.

source_uses.usable_for: Concrete program details (340 trees, 212 complaints, 2,300 pounds to pantries), the stewardship cost comparison, and a proposal to shift plantings from sidewalks to parks; usable by pro, con and conditional positions.

The strongest opposition: seasonality versus year-round hunger, unequal access to the harvest, liability and mess, and the alternative of shade trees plus food-bank funding; also a target for rebuttal.

The conditional case: contrast of unrequested sidewalk pears with a requested park grove, 'polite fruit' species choice, the 'no steward, no tree' rule, and organized harvest practices that answer fairness objections.
The social and intangible benefits (neighbors meeting, children learning where food comes from), an honest concession about mess, and a claim that unmeasurable goods still justify planting.

Public support that depends on location (68 percent parks versus 41 percent streets), the gap between approval and actual harvesting (23 percent), widespread worry about mess (57 percent), low volunteer willingness (29 percent) and uncertainty about safety (32 percent unsure).

Cost evidence: shade trees cost 48 dollars, stewarded fruit trees 71, unstewarded 112, nut trees 64 and 98; supports arguments that stewardship or species choice, not fruit itself, determines the burden, and that nut trees are cheaper than fruit trees.

common_pitfalls: Writing a thesis that says public orchards have 'advantages and disadvantages' without choosing a position.
Organizing the essay source by source (a paragraph on A, then B, then C) instead of around the writer's own claims.
Quoting Source D's warm anecdote without acknowledging that a personal essay about one tree is not evidence about a whole program.
Citing a number from Source E or F without saying what it demonstrates, or confusing approval of park plantings (68 percent) with willingness to volunteer (29 percent).
Treating Source B's op-ed as neutral fact rather than as an argument with its own rhetorical aims.
Ignoring the location distinction (sidewalk versus park) that runs through Sources A, C and E, which collapses the most useful conditional position into a simple pro or con.
Using the sources as decoration for an opinion formed in advance rather than letting them shape and complicate the position.

samples.essay:
Every city has trees that nobody really owns. They belong to "the public," which in practice means whichever parks crew gets the phone calls. Fruit trees make that problem obvious, because a plum tree nobody cares for doesn't just stand there. It drops its fruit on somebody's shoe. Cities should plant fruit and nut trees on public land, but only in parks, schoolyards and library lawns, and only where a group of residents has signed on to care for the trees and share the harvest before the tree goes in. The tree is the easy part. The people are the actual program.

The strongest evidence for this is the stewardship numbers. In Marlow Bend, a fruit tree with a volunteer steward costs the city 71 dollars a year, and one with no steward costs 112 dollars (Source A, Source F). That 41 dollars gap is almost the entire cost of an ordinary shade tree (48 dollars). So an unloved fruit tree costs more than twice as much as a shade tree, but a cared-for one costs only about 23 dollars more. Nut trees show the same pattern, 64 dollars versus 98. dollars Superintendent Threlkeld puts it bluntly: trees without a block captain "look like nobody loves them, because nobody does." Palumbo in Verrin Heights (Source C) learned the same lesson from both directions. His grant-funded sidewalk pears are "the ugliest trees we own," while the grove a seniors' club asked for at Thistle Park became "the best trees we own." His rule, "no steward, no tree," is basically the cost chart turned into a policy.

Location matters almost as much as stewardship. Caddis Falls residents support fruit trees in parks 68 percent to 19, but on residential streets they split 41 to 44 (Source E). That doesn't mean people hate fruit. It means they don't want plums on the sidewalk in front of their own house. Council member Adebanjo-Lind voted for the Marlow Bend program, but he now says "a plum tree over a bus stop was a mistake," which is the same line the survey draws. Palumbo's "polite fruit," like persimmons that hang on until someone picks them, takes care of a lot of the mess complaint too.

Ashby-Feld (Source B) makes the best case against, and he is right about some things. A three-week plum season is not a food policy, and a hungry family needs a pantry that's open in February. But his column is an opinion piece aimed at the weakest version of the idea: a sidewalk plum with no plan behind it. His most serious point is fairness, that the harvest goes to "whoever has a ladder." Palumbo, though, describes the fixes for exactly that: loaner poles for people who can't climb, a chalkboard of picking dates, and a rule that the first basket goes to the Ferrow Street pantry. Ashby-Feld sees the race and decides not to plant. Palumbo sees the same race and decides to organize it. And since the Boulevard Gleaners carried 2,300 pounds of fruit to church pantries, the trees and the food bank don't have to be rivals.

Still, the steward rule has a cost I don't want to skip over. Only 29 percent of Caddis Falls residents say they would volunteer (Source E). The neighborhoods most likely to have a seniors' club with free afternoons may not be the ones that need free fruit the most. Left alone, "no steward, no tree" could put orchards mainly in neighborhoods that are already organized. So cities should help create stewards instead of just waiting for them to show up, for example by pairing a school or library with a local pantry.

This matters because, as Marrow writes in Source D, the fruit is really "the excuse." Her shy daughter and Mr. Haldane only met because of a serviceberry. Her essay is one family's story, and only 23 percent of residents picked anything last year, so I wouldn't build a budget on it. But it explains something the cost chart can't, which is why a city might pay that extra 23. dollars Shade falls on everyone equally, like Ashby-Feld says, but it has never gotten two strangers talking.

samples.essay:
Cities should plant fruit and nut trees on public land, but only in parks and school grounds where a volunteer group has agreed to take care of them. Planting them along sidewalks or without anyone in charge causes more problems than it solves.

The biggest reason is cost and mess. In Source A, Marlow Bend replaced its ash trees with edible ones and got 212 service requests in one year, mostly about plums staining sidewalks and attracting wasps. The superintendent says that trees with a block captain look great and the others look like nobody loves them. Source F backs this up with numbers, since a fruit tree with a steward costs 71 dollars a year but one without a steward costs 112, which is more than double the 48 dollars for an ordinary shade tree. This shows that the trees themselves are not the main expense, it is the lack of people looking after them. So if a city plants fruit trees with no plan for who cares for them, it ends up paying a lot more.

Source C makes the same point from a different city. Palumbo's pears downtown were planted because of a grant and nobody asked for them, so they became the ugliest trees he has. The Thistle Park grove, which a seniors' club asked for and signed an agreement about, became the best. His rule of "no steward, no tree" fits my position well. It also answers part of what Source B complains about. Ashby-Feld says the fruit goes to whoever has a ladder and a free Saturday, but Palumbo says Thistle Park has loaner poles and a chalkboard of picking dates, so organization can fix the fairness problem.

However, I have to admit Source B has a point that is harder to answer. A plum tree fruits for three weeks and hunger lasts all year, so public orchards are not a real food policy. Source E also gives a warning, because only 23 percent of residents picked any public fruit and only 29 percent would volunteer. That means finding stewards might be hard, and the steward rule could mean few trees get planted. But I think that is actually fine, since the survey also shows 68 percent support trees in parks while only 41 percent support them on streets. People seem to already understand that parks are the better place.

Source D shows what the trees can give besides food. Marrow met Mr. Haldane because of a serviceberry by the library, something that she says a city cannot measure. This is a personal essay so it is not hard evidence, but it shows why a small number of well-run trees is worth it even if they do not feed the city.

In conclusion, cities should plant edible trees, but in parks, schools and libraries, with a steward group that signs on first.

ALTON original passage
Where the Play Depends on You
Marisol Quade, remarks to the student technical crew of Harrow Bend High School, delivered on the stage after the final dress rehearsal, April 2019

¶1 (1) Thirty-one years ago I stood where you are standing, holding a roll of glow tape and wondering why I had signed up for a job nobody would clap for. (2) Tomorrow night four hundred people will fill those seats, and not one of them will know your names. (3) They will not see the forty feet of cable you coiled this afternoon, or the sandbag you re-tied twice because the first knot felt wrong, or the three-second hole in the second act that you closed with a flashlight and a whisper. (4) Good.

¶2 (5) I know what some of you are thinking, because I thought it too. (6) Why spend six weeks building a world for other people to stand in? (7) Why learn the choreography of a scene change you perform in total darkness? (8) The answer I would have given at seventeen was that someone had to do it. (9) The answer I give now is different: the dark is not where the play hides from you; it is where the play depends on you.

¶3 (10) Let me tell you about a girl named Theodora Vance, who ran the fly rail for a production of a storm play at the old Carrow Street Playhouse in 1994. (11) In the third act a painted sky was supposed to drop in on a count of eight. (12) The actor jumped his cue by half a page, and the storm he was describing to the audience had not arrived. (13) Theodora did not panic, did not wait for me, did not check the book. (14) She brought the sky in on the line, early, perfectly, and the audience gasped at the weather. (15) The review the next morning praised the actor's uncanny timing. (16) Theodora read that review on the bus and, as she told me later, laughed until the driver asked if she was all right.

¶4 (17) That laugh is the whole job. (18) A stage crew is the circulatory system of a production: nobody admires it, nobody photographs it, and the moment it stops, everything on the surface turns gray. (19) The actors are the face; you are the pulse. The night before opening, after a long dress rehearsal, a tired high school crew does not need to be told their work is glamorous, because they know it isn't. Marisol Quade seems to understand this. Instead of promising the crew recognition they will never get, she redefines invisibility, turning it from an insult into proof that they did the job right. Quade opens by standing where the students stand. "Thirty-one years ago I stood where you are standing" gives her authority, but it also tells the crew she once felt the same way, "wondering why I had signed up for a job nobody would clap for." Then she lists what they actually did that day: "the forty feet of cable you coiled this afternoon," the sandbag "re-tied twice because the first knot felt wrong." The students' complaint is that nobody notices, and in the first paragraph a speaker shows that she noticed. Then comes the one-word sentence "Good." After a long, heavy list, it is jarring, and I think it's meant to be. The crew expects sympathy and gets a challenge, which makes them want to hear why being unnoticed could possibly be good.

Next she says their doubts out loud. "Why spend six weeks building a world for other people to stand in?" Because she admits "some of you are thinking" this, nobody has to complain, and she gets to answer them directly. Her answer is an antithesis: "the dark is not where the play hides from you; it is where the play depends on you." For a crew, "the dark" means being hidden, and she flips it so it means being trusted.

The Theodora story makes that flip concrete. When the actor jumped his cue, Theodora "did not panic, did not wait for me, did not check the book," and the next day's review praised "the actor's uncanny timing." rows.task_specific: Observing that the talk ends with practical instructions ('check your headset') rather than a grand flourish, and explaining why that understatement fits a speaker who values unseen work, is one route to this point.

scoring_notes: Essays that misidentify a device (calling the circulatory-system comparison a simile) are not penalized if the commentary on its effect is accurate.
Paragraph-by-paragraph summary with occasional device names earns at most 2 on Row B.

An essay that discusses only one choice in depth can earn a 3 on Row B if the commentary is specific and tied to purpose, but a 4 requires more than one choice and a line of reasoning across the passage.
Do not reward length; a short essay with precise commentary on three choices outscores a long essay that lists eight.
The sophistication point is not earned by a sweeping conclusion about the importance of teamwork or by using the word 'juxtaposition' without explaining the effect.

defensible_positions: Quade reframes invisibility from a loss into evidence of success by voicing the crew's doubts, answering them with a concrete story and a bodily metaphor, and then admitting the cost before converting the argument into a closing instruction.
Quade builds credibility by positioning herself as a former doubter and a once-slighted crew member, so that her praise of unseen work reads as earned rather than sentimental.
Quade moves the crew from discouragement to readiness through a shift from question and anecdote to confession and command.
lines_of_reasoning: Doubt voiced (6 to 7), doubt answered by example (10 to 16), answer generalized by metaphor (18 to 22), objection conceded and overturned (23 to 28), argument turned into action (29 to 33).
Three redefinitions of 'thanks': the review that credits the wrong person (15), the thanks 'already in the room' (26), and the instruction to thank each other (32).
Credibility built by shared experience: Quade stood where they stand (1), thought what they think (5), wanted what they want (24), and still chose the booth.

rhetorical_choices.effect: Establishes Quade as someone who once held the same doubts in the same position, so the crew hears her as a peer who stayed rather than an authority lecturing them.
A long inventory of unseen tasks is cut off by the single word 'Good,' which jolts the crew by treating the thing they fear as the goal.
Welcoming invisibility, the review that credits the actor, and work that is not magic but looks like it all train the crew to read lack of credit as a sign of success.
Puts the crew's unspoken complaint into Quade's own mouth so she can answer it instead of dismissing it.
Balanced oppositions (hides/depends, face/pulse, applause/invisibility) make her reframing sound like a settled truth rather than consolation.
Colons set up each key claim as a revelation, slowing the crew down right before the line she most wants remembered.
A specific, named crew member saving a show and laughing at the misdirected praise gives the crew a model of how to feel, not just what to believe.
The tripled 'did not' conveys Theodora's composure and implicitly lists the instincts the crew must suppress tomorrow.
Comparing the crew to the circulatory system makes invisibility a property of vital things rather than unimportant ones, and 'pulse' gives them a dignified role opposite the actors' 'face.'

Concrete numbers drawn from the crew's own month make the argument about their work rather than about crews in general, and the silent trapdoor shows that their best work is defined by what the audience will not notice.
Admitting that going unthanked stings, with a specific memory of the slighted booth, prevents the talk from sounding naive and makes the rebuttal about thanks 'already in the room' more trustworthy.
The short confession and the drive home with the radio off let the crew see their own hurt reflected in a veteran, which lowers their defenses before the turn.
The voice moves from confessional to brisk and commanding, carrying the crew out of reflection and into the readiness opening night requires.
Second-person commands make the crew participants rather than listeners and end the talk as a cue rather than a speech.
Setting 'No one will ever thank you' directly against 'Thank each other' gives the crew a substitute for the applause they will not get.
Ending with a routine headset check rather than a flourish enacts the talk's own value: the important thing is the quiet, practical work.

source_uses.usable_for: All evidence for the rhetorical analysis essay.

common_pitfalls: Treating the talk as an essay about theater and arguing whether crew work is valued, rather than analyzing how Quade argues.
Listing devices paragraph by paragraph with the same generic effect ('this makes the audience feel connected') for each.
Ignoring the audience: forgetting that the listeners are tired high school students, which is why Quade uses their own inventory of work in sentence 20 and ends with a plain instruction.
Quoting sentence 18 and labeling it a metaphor without explaining why 'circulatory system' (vital, invisible, fatal if it stops) is a fitting comparison for her purpose.
Overlooking the concession in paragraph five or treating it as a weakness in the argument rather than as a deliberate credibility move.
Claiming the anecdote is 'pathos' without explaining what the laugh on the bus is meant to teach the crew about how to feel when the credit goes elsewhere.

The night before opening, after a long dress rehearsal, a tired high school crew does not need to be told their work is glamorous, because they know it isn't. Marisol Quade seems to understand this. Instead of promising the crew recognition they will never get, she redefines invisibility, turning it from an insult into proof that they did the job right. She builds this in stages: she voices the crew's complaints for them, answers those complaints with a story and a metaphor that make unseen work feel essential, and then admits the arrangement hurts, so that her final commands sound like advice from someone who has been there and not like a pep talk.

Quade opens by standing where the students stand. "Thirty-one years ago I stood where you are standing" gives her authority, but it also tells the crew she once felt the same way, "wondering why I had signed up for a job nobody would clap for." Then she lists what they actually did that day: "the forty feet of cable you coiled this afternoon," the sandbag "re-tied twice because the first knot felt wrong." The students' complaint is that nobody notices, and in the first paragraph a speaker shows that she noticed. Then comes the one-word sentence "Good." After a long, heavy list, it is jarring, and I think it's meant to be. The crew expects sympathy and gets a challenge, which makes them want to hear why being unnoticed could possibly be good.

Next she says their doubts out loud. "Why spend six weeks building a world for other people to stand in?" Because she admits "some of you are thinking" this, nobody has to complain, and she gets to answer them directly. Her answer is an antithesis: "the dark is not where the play hides from you; it is where the play depends on you." For a crew, "the dark" means being hidden, and she flips it so it means being trusted.

The Theodora story makes that flip concrete. When the actor jumped his cue, Theodora "did not panic, did not wait for me, did not check the book," and the next day's review praised "the actor's uncanny timing." The irony is obvious, since the credit went to the wrong person, but Theodora laughs instead of resenting it. "That laugh is the whole job," Quade says, meaning the crew gets to know a secret the audience doesn't. The circulatory-system metaphor pushes this further: "The actors are the face; you are the pulse." Students who feel minor are told they are the part a body can't live without. Even her count, "two hundred and six lighting cues," does what the audience won't, which is to add up their work.

What makes the speech convincing, though, is that Quade doesn't pretend this is all fine. "I will admit the arrangement is not fair," she says, and she remembers the night in Lissenbrook when she "drove home with the radio off." If she had only said invisibility is a reward, teenagers who feel cheated would probably hear an adult explaining away something unfair. By admitting it stung, she holds both ideas together. "Invisibility is the proof that you did it right" comes after the hurt, not instead of it, so the crew can believe it without having to pretend they aren't disappointed.

The ending finishes the argument without a big flourish. "No one will ever thank you for it. Thank each other." Since thanks won't come from the audience, she gives the crew a replacement they control. Then: "Then check your headset, and let's go." A speech about work nobody sees ends on a small, practical task instead of a grand line. That understatement suits a speaker who values quiet competence, and it turns the crew's discouragement back toward the job in front of them.

In her talk to the Harrow Bend tech crew, Marisol Quade uses personal experience, a story, and a metaphor to change how the students think about being unseen, so that what feels like a loss becomes something to be proud of. Her audience is tired and discouraged, so she has to do more than just tell them their work matters.

Quade starts by building her credibility. She says "Thirty-one years ago I stood where you are standing, holding a roll of glow tape," which tells the students she was once in their position and was a crew member too. This matters because teenagers who feel overlooked might not listen to someone who has never felt that way. Then she lists the things the audience will not see, like the cable and the sandbag, and ends with the single word "Good." The word is short compared to the long sentence before it, and it surprises the crew because it makes not being noticed sound like the goal. She also asks questions like "Why spend six weeks building a world for other people to stand in?" These questions say out loud what the students have been complaining about, so they know she is listening to them.

The biggest part of her argument is the story of Theodora Vance. Theodora saved the show by dropping the sky in early when the actor missed his cue, but the review praised the actor instead. Quade says Theodora "laughed until the driver asked if she was all right." This example shows the crew that someone who was not credited could still be happy about it. It also proves that crew work can be very important, since the audience gasped at the weather. Quade then follows up with the metaphor that the crew is "the circulatory system" and the actors are the face while "you are the pulse." This comparison shows that something can be necessary even if nobody admires it. She also lists what the crew did this month, such as "two hundred and six lighting cues," which gives them specific proof of their work.

Quade also admits that it is not fair. She says "I would be lying if I told you it never stung" and tells about the night in Lissenbrook when the booth was skipped at the cast party. By admitting this she seems honest, so the students are more likely to believe her when she says "Invisibility is the proof that you did it right." She does not just give a pep talk, she shows she has felt what they feel.

At the end the tone changes and she gives commands, "listen," "Thank each other," and "check your headset." The ending is practical and not dramatic, which fits the crew's job of doing small things well. Overall, Quade gets the students ready for opening night by showing them their invisible work is a kind of success.

payload.title: Whose Step Is It? Shared Responsibility for Public Sidewalks and Stairs
payload.set_intro:
ALTON original passage

Nobody's Child
Delia Marchbank, column in the Fallow Ridge Weekly Courier

In many hillside towns, the stairs and sidewalks that stitch one street to the next are nobody's child. The city claims them on its maps and forgets them in its budget; the people who live beside them sweep the leaves off some mornings and step over the broken risers on others. Some residents argue that the fix is obvious: if you live on a block, you owe it your shovel, your rake, and a Saturday now and then. Others answer that this is exactly what taxes are for, and that asking neighbors to patch public concrete lets officials off the hook while quietly penalizing the elderly, the renters, and the people working two jobs. A third camp says the truth sits in the middle: neighbors should keep things passable, but anything involving rebar is the city's problem. Who, in the end, owns a public step?

parts.label: A
parts.prompt:
In a column for a small-town weekly, commentator Delia Marchbank wrote the following about the hillside stairways and sidewalks that connect the streets of her town.

Write an essay that argues your position on the extent to which the residents of a neighborhood should share responsibility for maintaining the public sidewalks and steps that run through it.

Your essay should:
- Respond to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible position.
- Provide evidence to support your line of reasoning, drawing on your reading, experience, or observations.
- Explain how the evidence supports your line of reasoning, and use appropriate strategies to develop and organize your argument.
parts.model_answer:
On my grandmother's street there is a set of forty-one concrete steps that runs down from Linden Avenue to the bus stop on Carver. I know it's forty-one because I counted them once while carrying her groceries, and also because step twenty-six has been cracked in half for as long as I can remember. The people on Linden shovel those steps after almost every snow. Nobody has ever fixed step twenty-six. To me that staircase answers Marchbank's question better than any of her three camps. Residents should do the light, everyday work that keeps a public step usable, like sweeping, shoveling, and salting. But that duty is only fair if the city keeps the structure itself safe, and it should fall mostly on the people who own property along the steps, not on every resident equally.

First, why should neighbors owe anything at all? Because they're the ones who are there. When it snowed eight inches last January, the city plows cleared Carver by noon, but they don't plow stairs. If Mr. Dunleavy at the top hadn't been out with his shovel at seven, the nurses and kids who take the 6 bus would have been sliding down ice. Shoveling takes twenty minutes and needs no permit and no engineer. A city crew would have to be scheduled and paid and sent across town, and by the time they showed up the snow would have turned into a sheet of ice. For small jobs like this, the person closest to the problem can fix it the fastest, and that's a pretty good reason to make it their job.

Step twenty-six shows where that reasoning stops working, though. You can't shovel your way out of broken concrete, and the neighbors' shoveling actually hides the problem. Since the steps always look cared for, nobody files a complaint, and the city never puts them on a repair list. This is the danger of the "it's your block, it's your shovel" argument. The more neighbors do, the less the city feels it has to do, until the residents are basically holding up infrastructure they don't own. So my position comes with a condition. Neighbors keep the steps passable, the city keeps them standing, and if the city stops doing its part, neighbors shouldn't be expected to just keep sweeping around the crack.

The strongest objection is the one Marchbank mentions about the elderly, renters, and people working two jobs. It's a real problem. My grandmother is eighty-three, and expecting her to shovel forty-one steps would be dangerous and also unfair. The family renting the triplex might be gone by next winter, so they have little reason to invest in a block they won't stay on. That's why I don't think the duty should belong to "residents" in general. It should belong to owners. Homeowners and landlords are the ones whose property values go up when a neighborhood is walkable, so they benefit the most from the steps being kept up. A landlord can hire someone or write shoveling into a lease. Renters and older neighbors can pitch in if they want to, but a rule that fines them for not shoveling would punish the people with the least time and money for something everybody uses.

Underneath all of this is the question of what a public step even is. If it belongs to everyone in an abstract way, it ends up belonging to nobody, which is how step twenty-six stays broken. But if it belongs completely to the people next to it, it starts to feel like their private property, and that isn't right either, since the woman from three streets over walking to the bus has just as much right to it. I think a public step works more like a library book. The city buys it and repairs it, and the people using it every day are expected to keep it in good shape. Neither one can do the other's job, and the staircase on Linden is what happens when only one side does its part.

rubric_rows.criterion: Qualified theses count fully as long as they draw a real line: for example, 'residents should handle routine upkeep but never structural repair,' or 'shared upkeep is fair only where the city first makes the infrastructure safe.' A thesis that says 'it depends on the situation' without naming what it depends on does not earn the point.

Acceptable evidence includes personal observation of a block or building, experience with volunteer or civic work, historical or literary examples of commons and shared upkeep, hypothetical but concrete scenarios, and reasoning from principles of fairness, safety, or liability. Evidence need not be factual in the statistical sense; it must be specific and tied to the claim. Do not reward essays for quoting Marchbank at length; the stimulus is a springboard, not a source to be analyzed.

The sophistication point most often comes from an essay that explains the limits of its own position: who it would unfairly burden, what would happen if everyone followed it, or how it depends on a city holding up its end. Award it for insight embedded in the argument, not for a closing paragraph that gestures at nuance.
